transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 45 minutes — quick hello?
[00:05] Priya Anand: Hi, thanks — Priya here.
[00:07] Marco Rossi: Marco, hi.
[00:09] Elena Petrova: Elena.
[00:11] Liam Chen: Liam from Redwood, hi all.
[00:13] Jamal Turner: Jamal, security.
[00:15] Sofia: Cool. Quick agenda — last week's bench runs, SDK integration questions, structured output format for our transaction enrichment, and security asks. Liam, want to kick off with the SDK notes?
[00:28] Liam: Yep. So we pushed the sample SDK that does function-calling and structured output — link in the notes, redwood.ai/sdk -> I know the transcript sometimes garbles links, but it's in the follow-up email. The important bit: the Node and Python SDKs support two paths: regular chat/generate and explicit function/tool calling. For your use case Marco, you want the tool call where the model returns a JSON object that maps to your enrichment pipeline.
[00:51] Marco: Right — our backend expects a strict schema: merchant_name, merchant_id, category_code, confidence_score (0-1), and optional flags. We need the model to always return JSON and fail loudly if it doesn't.
[01:05] Liam: Understood. In the SDK sample we show how to provide a function signature — basically a JSON schema — and set the call to "required_response_format": "json_schema". That forces structured output. There's also post-validate hooks in the SDK so you get a structured object or a parse error.
[01:22] Elena: Quick question — what's the difference between that and just parsing the model text output?
[01:27] Liam: Two things — one, the function-calling gives the model an explicit contract, which reduces hallucinations and formatting drift. Two, the SDK validates and will return a parse error rather than a malformed string, which makes your pipeline safer.
[01:40] Priya: We saw last week that about 8% of responses needed manual cleanup when we tried naive regex parsing. So the contract would be a big plus.
[01:48] Sofia: Can you show the code snippet briefly?
[01:50] Liam: Yeah — high level: you register a function definition in the SDK with name, input schema, required fields and datatypes. Then when you call generate, you include that function list and set mode to "function_prefer" or "function_required". If required, the model must emit a function result. Sample code is in the repo — I'll paste exact snippet after the call.
[02:08] Marco: Are there any costs or latency tradeoffs when you force function_required?
[02:13] Liam: Minimal — the model still generates tokens. Function enforcement is mostly a post-processing step in the SDK. However, to increase accuracy we sometimes recommend longer context (more system + examples), which increases tokens. So tradeoff is token cost vs accuracy. For p95 latency, in our dedicated pool we saw ~150-220ms per call on the small LLM variant when using standard 512-token contexts. In hosted sandbox your numbers may be higher depending on token sizes.
[02:40] Marco: That p95 number is much better than we expected, nice. Our SLA target is 250ms for the enrichment path.
[02:47] Liam: Should be achievable with batching and prefix caching. We'll share config suggestions — in particular the batching window and KV cache warmup.
[02:56] Priya: On caching — our user flows are highly variable; we can't always rely on prefix matching. Any suggestions?
[03:03] Liam: For variable prompts, you can still get wins from partial KV caching — caching model key-values for common system prompts and examples. Also do request-level caching for identical transactions — the SDK supports a cache key you can define. We'll include an example.
[03:20] Jamal: Security — quick: where are the logs stored? We need audit logs and control over retention.
[03:24] Sofia: For the pilot we're on hosted but with restricted retention. We can configure retention windows and send audit logs to your SIEM via our webhook integration. You also asked for KMS integration — we support customer-managed keys for the private plane (VPC) and Dedicated. We'll share the SOC2 artifact bundle.
[03:40] Jamal: Good. Also need to know about data residency — EU-only. Is that available?
[03:44] Liam: Yes — we have EU regions and can pin the pilot to eu-west-1. For Private deployments we can support on-prem too but that's a later phase.
[03:52] Elena: Back to structured output — what happens when the model returns a field with wrong type, like string instead of float for confidence_score?
[03:58] Liam: SDK validation will flag type mismatch and return an error object with the raw contents. You can configure fallback policies — e.g., attempt numeric cast, or route to a low-confidence manual review queue. We can show a recommended policy: reject above 0.7 confidence automatically, below go to review.
[04:15] Marco: For our pipeline, we want to automatically accept only when confidence_score > 0.85. Anything else goes to review. Can we set that in Redwood routing?
[04:21] Sofia: Yes — routing rules can be set in the console or via API; you can define thresholds for auto-accept and even route to a canary model. We'll include a sample route policy.
[04:32] Priya: About function/tool calling — we plan to call an internal enrichment microservice for entity resolution. Could we have the Redwood model trigger a webhook or call a tool to do lookups?
[04:42] Liam: Absolutely — the "tool" interface allows you to register external tools. In the SDK you declare a tool with an endpoint and auth; the runtime can call out and wait for the tool result, which then becomes part of the model context. For strict security you can keep that tool inside your VPC and use the private connector.
[04:58] Marco: Are those tool calls synchronous and do they add to latency?
[05:02] Liam: They are by default synchronous — so they add the tool execution time to the overall response. In practice we keep the tool latency under 50ms; if your microservice is slower, consider returning a placeholder and running an async enrichment pipeline, or using batching.
[05:17] Elena: One gotcha we hit: when the tool returns null fields the model sometimes still fills them in with guesses. Any pattern to prevent that?
[05:25] Liam: We recommend conservative system prompts and explicit instructions: "if tool response is null, return null for those fields" and make the schema mark fields nullable. There's also a parameter to prefer tool data over model hallucinated content.
[05:39] Marco: On implementation, Marco: in our backend we use Go; any SDK support?
[05:45] Liam: We have official Node and Python SDKs but also HTTP REST endpoints; you can call the API directly from Go. We also have community-contrib Go client. For the POC, we usually provide a thin wrapper — we'll include an example curl and Go snippet.
[06:00] Priya: Token accounting — last week your sandbox showed ~220 tokens per enrichment call on average. That was with 3 examples in context. Can we reduce tokens without losing accuracy?
[06:10] Liam: Yes — strategies: reduce examples, use shorter system prompt, or switch to a smaller model and then apply a reranker or specialized smaller classifier for final accept/reject. There's also structured prompts: send serialized key-value instead of long narrative. We'll send a few experiment configs.
[06:28] Marco: For reranker, do you support secondary calls like embedding-based similarity?
[06:33] Liam: Embeddings and reranking are supported — you can run a cheap embedding compare or a small ranking model; Redwood Optimize can recommend thresholds and even tune quantization to reduce cost.
[06:43] Sofia: Quick check — your acceptance criteria for the POC? Priya?
[06:47] Priya: 1) integration completes end-to-end, 2) p95 enrichment latency under 250ms, 3) accuracy with false positive rate under 3% on a sample set, 4) security artifacts provided.
[07:00] Sofia: Great. We'll align the action items to that.
[07:04] Jamal: On security artifacts — I need the SOC2 Type II report, ISO summary, and the ingress/egress network topology for the pilot.
[07:12] Sofia: Noted — I'll drop those in the shared folder.
[07:15] Liam: I'll paste the SDK snippet now — rough pseudo:
[07:19] Liam: // Node example
[07:21] Liam: const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY });
[07:25] Liam: const func = { name: 'enrich_transaction', schema: { type: 'object', properties: { merchant_name: { type: 'string' }, merchant_id: { type: 'string' }, category_code: { type: 'string' }, confidence_score: { type: 'number' } }, required: ['merchant_name','merchant_id','confidence_score'] } };
[07:44] Liam: const res = await client.generate({ model:'redwood-small', input: prompt, functions: [func], functionMode:'required', outputFormat:'json_schema' });
[07:53] Liam: // SDK returns either { success: true, data: { ... } } or { success:false, errors: [...] }
[07:58] Marco: That looks good. Will you include sample error objects?
[08:01] Liam: Yes — we'll include both type-mismatch and missing-required examples.
[08:05] Elena: About monitoring — how do we get token-level cost breakdowns?
[08:09] Aisha: Console has per-route metrics and token heatmaps. For pilot we'll give you a token-level export and a spreadsheet with the sample runs.
[08:18] Marco: Please include p50/p95 for both generation and overall request with tool latency included.
[08:23] Sofia: Will do.
[08:25] Priya: Anything about rate-limits? For initial pilot we may burst 200 qps.
[08:29] Liam: For hosted we can provision burst capacity; for sustained 200 qps we recommend Dedicated. For pilot you'll get modest burst with rate-limits — we'll simulate your burst in our bench if you share expected distributions.
[08:42] Marco: Ok we'll share a traffic sample.
[08:45] Jamal: One more security note — we require SAML SSO and SCIM user provisioning for any console access.
[08:51] Sofia: Supported — we'll send SSO setup docs.
[08:54] Elena: Any gotchas for structured outputs in low-content cases, like sparse transaction descriptions?
[08:59] Liam: When input lacks signal, confidence falls — consider fallback to rule-based heuristics or call a heavier model for those cases. Router can route based on confidence.
[09:10] Marco: For the next run, we will try two configs: A) smaller model + reranker, B) larger model with function_required. We'll capture accuracy and cost.
[09:20] Sofia: Great. Recap of immediate deliverables? Liam to share SDK snippets and schema examples; Sofia to send pricing and security artifacts; Marco to run bench and send results; Jamal to list compliance docs.
[09:34] Priya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:36] Sofia: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links and the action-item list.
[09:40] Marco: Bye.
[09:41] Liam: Bye.
[09:42] End of recording.
